title: Environmental Alert: A new MAAP report reveals that 15% of the original Amazon rainforest has been lost - Noticias Ambientales
text:
Environmental Alert: A new MAAP report reveals that 15% of the original Amazon rainforest has been lost - Noticias Ambientales 
 Type your search query and hit enter: Categories: Science Environmental Alert: A new MAAP report reveals that 15% of the original Amazon rainforest has been lost
 perdida de bosque en el Amazonas 
 A new report from the Monitoring of the Andean Amazon Program (MAAP) by Amazon Conservation reveals that 15% of the original primary forest of the Amazon basin has already disappeared.
 The losses are concentrated along the moisture routes on which some regions depend more heavily.
 97 million hectares lost by 2025
 The report MAAP #250: Amazon Tipping Point: Where Are We? (2026 Update) estimates that 97.06 million hectares of primary forest were lost in the nine countries of the biome by the end of 2025. The main causes are deforestation and fires caused by humans.
 The total loss increased from 13.2% in 2021, according to the first assessment (MAAP #164), to 15% by 2025. Between 2022 and 2025 alone, an additional 13.04 million hectares were lost, an area almost 15 times larger than Yellowstone National Park. This includes record losses due to fires in 2024, following the strong El Niño season of 2023.
 This loss brings the Amazon closer to its tipping point , which according to scientific literature could be triggered with a loss of around 25% , combined with the impacts of climate change .
 Moisture routes, the most affected
 The analysis breaks down the loss along the seasonal rivers that carry water in the Amazon. The dry and transition season routes lost almost three times more forest than the wet season route. These routes sustain the forests of the southwestern Amazon, in Peru and Bolivia , where more than 70% of the rainfall depends on moisture recycled by forests throughout the basin.
 The numbers by route:
 Wet season: 3.2% forest loss.
 Transition season: 9.1%.
 Dry season: 8.6%.
 The report on forest loss in the Amazon highlights the urgency to act against deforestation and fires. El Niño exacerbates the urgency
 The findings become more urgent with the forecast of a very intense El Niño , expected to strengthen by the end of 2026. MAAP #248 suggests it could alter the moisture flow of the rainy season, extend the dry and transition seasons, and increase the risk of wildfires . These are the same regions whose routes are already the most deforested.
 Matt Finer , director of MAAP and senior specialist at Amazon Conservation, stated that “media reports often generally indicate that the Amazon is approaching a critical point, but these are the real data that reveal the magnitude of the problem.” He added that “we are approaching the point where the hydrological cycle that sustains the rainforests could be permanently disrupted.”
 What is the tipping point and why is it not uniform
 The hypothesis suggests that some jungle areas could turn into a drier savanna when deforestation reaches 25% and climate change alters rainfall. However, the threshold is not definitive: changes can be gradual and fragmented, and the risk varies throughout the Amazon.
 The 2022 analysis showed this variation. With a total loss of 13.2%, the eastern third (mainly the Brazilian Amazon) had already lost about 30.8% , above the hypothetical threshold. The central third had lost 10.8% and the western third, 6.3%.
 The “flying rivers” and the domino effect
 The jungle generates about half of its own rain and recycles moisture up to six times through atmospheric flows called flying rivers . These transport moisture from the Atlantic westward. Trees take water from the soil and return it to the atmosphere as vapor, which sustains rainfall up to the Andes .
 Therefore, cutting down forests in one area can reduce the moisture reaching downwind regions and threaten ecosystems that depend on recycled rain. It is unlikely that the tipping point will be a single, uniform event: it could develop over decades and differently in each region.
 Previous research (MAAP #232 and the 2026 technical report “Maintaining the River’s Flow”) identified the southwestern Amazon as particularly vulnerable. In the dry and transition seasons, the moisture reaching there crosses heavily deforested areas of the Brazilian Amazon, such as the Pará region.
 Brazil accounts for 79% of the loss
 The update uses the same baseline as MAAP #164: an original forest of 647.6 million hectares . Of the 97.06 million lost, 84.28 million were due to deforestation and other non-fire-related causes, and 12.78 million to fires.
 By country:
 Brazil: 79.4%.
 Bolivia: 6.2%, now second, after being fourth in 2022.
 Peru: 5.8%.
 Colombia: 4.5%.
 A connected forest requires connected science and conservation
 According to the reports, understanding the tipping point requires more than estimating how much forest has been lost: it is necessary to know where it occurs, how it interacts with moisture cycles, and which regions depend most on recycled rain.
 With the pressure of deforestation, fires, and climate change, it is essential to view the Amazon as an interconnected system and not as isolated forests separated by borders. “A connected forest requires interconnected science and conservation.”
